My role

What I led

I served as team lead on CrashGuard, owning the technical direction of the build and the effort to make its measurements trustworthy.

  • Own the detection firmware. Wrote and tuned the ESP32/MPU6050 firmware that recovers dynamic acceleration from the raw accelerometer counts, detects impact events in real time, and autonomously triggers the emergency call.
  • Architected the tech stack. Defined the full signal-to-action chain end to end (on-vehicle sensing, the BLE link to a phone with its Wi-Fi HTTP fallback, the Flask call server and dashboard, and the Twilio voice interface), resolving the threading and timeout failures that blocked reliable real-time dispatch.
  • Led the team. Coordinated four engineers across firmware, host software, and demo preparation, keeping the subsystems integrating cleanly against the competition deadline.
  • Led the testing effort. Drove the work of getting accurate results rather than plausible ones: tracing the vendor library's sensor readings to their source, calibrating the gravity vector, and tuning the threshold and confirmation window so ordinary handling cannot raise an alert.
Problem

Why it exists

Every year, thousands of car crash victims suffer preventable deaths because emergency response is delayed, most critically when the driver is incapacitated and cannot call for help. CrashGuard closes that gap: it identifies a collision on its own from a sudden change in acceleration, then contacts help without requiring any action from the occupant.

The board becomes the "brain" of an in-vehicle guardian. When it detects an impact, a live phone dashboard flashes a ten-second countdown while the onboard buzzer sounds. A conscious occupant taps one big red CANCEL button and the system re-arms. If nobody cancels, CrashGuard assumes the occupant is incapacitated and escalates to an AI voice call that reports who they are, where they are, and what a dispatcher needs to know.

Prototype

Work-in-progress demo

Current prototype running end to end, impact detection, the cancel countdown on the phone dashboard, and the outbound AI call.

01

The chain of events

From impact to a dispatcher answering the phone, with a human override at the only point where one belongs.

  1. Detect. The accelerometer is sampled at 100 Hz; dynamic acceleration above 5.0 g on consecutive samples, or a sustained railed axis, declares a collision.
  2. Warn. The phone dashboard flashes !! CRASH DETECTED !! with a ten-second countdown and vibrates; the buzzer on the car beeps faster in the final three seconds.
  3. Offer the override. One tap on CANCEL - I'M OK dismisses the alert and re-arms the system, exactly how a conscious driver waves off a pothole.
  4. Escalate. If the countdown expires, the board pushes a Bluetooth alert to the host, which fires the call pipeline.
  5. Locate. A single batch of map lookups resolves the address, city, nearest cross streets, and closest hospitals from the live GPS fix.
  6. Call. Twilio places an outbound call that speaks the occupant's briefing, then a Claude agent answers the dispatcher's follow-up questions using only verified data.
  7. Document. After a few exchanges the system offers to send a full written incident report by SMS or email.
02

Impact detection

Subtracting the gravity vector, rather than its magnitude, makes the threshold pure excess acceleration and independent of mounting orientation.

Method

The MPU6050 accelerometer (I2C address 0x69) is sampled at 100 Hz with the full-scale range set to ±16 g. During a still-boot calibration the firmware averages one hundred samples to record the gravity vector g0, then subtracts it from every later sample to give the dynamic acceleration:

d(t) = (a(t) − g0) / |g0|

Because the whole vector is removed and not merely its magnitude, this reads 0.00 g at rest in any orientation. The threshold is therefore expressed purely as excess impact acceleration, with no gravity offset buried in the number. A collision is declared when the dynamic acceleration exceeds 5.0 g.

That value is chosen deliberately. Rotating the sensor by hand can produce at most 2 g of apparent dynamic acceleration, so any threshold above 2 g means ordinary handling can never raise an alert. Readings also pass through a median-of-three filter before comparison, which discards isolated outlier samples from bus glitches or transient saturation, so both the reported magnitude and the trigger reflect sustained motion rather than a single bad sample.

False positives are rejected by four mechanisms working together: gravity-vector removal, median-of-three spike filtering, the 5.0 g threshold, and a requirement for consecutive samples to confirm the event. GPS plays no part in this; it supplies location for the emergency call only.

Engineering lesson. Getting trustworthy acceleration required abandoning the vendor library's per-axis accessors. Reading its source revealed three properties that make them unsuitable for high-rate crash sensing. Each accessor re-reads the range configuration register, tripling I2C traffic at 100 Hz and returning intermittently corrupted samples. The three axes are read in separate transactions and therefore correspond to different instants, so their vector magnitude is not physically meaningful during rapid motion; the symptom was orientation-dependent readings of 14 to 17 g while the board sat perfectly still. And the library's scale factor is twice the correct value for every full-scale range, applying 2(fsr+1) where the datasheet requires 2fsr. The firmware now performs a single six-byte I2C burst read, so all three axes are sampled at the same instant, and applies the datasheet sensitivity of 2048 LSB/g at ±16 g to the raw counts directly. No gyroscope data is read at any point; angular rate is unnecessary for impact detection and would only add bus load. A vendor library being convenient does not make it correct at the rate you need, and reading the source is what turned a broken sensor into a reliable one.
Saturation

When the impact exceeds the instrument

Impacts on a rigid demonstration platform readily exceed the sensor's range, so sustained per-axis railing is treated as an independent crash indicator. When an axis reaches 95% of full scale for the confirmation window, an impact is declared regardless of the computed magnitude, and the alert is annotated to show that true severity exceeds the recorded peak. Collisions harder than the instrument can measure are therefore detected rather than missed.

Peaks

Two peaks, reported separately

The dashboard peak and the crash peak answer different questions, so they are measured differently:

  • Dashboard peak: holds the highest recent value for three seconds, then follows the live reading again, so the display reflects current activity rather than a stuck maximum.
  • Crash peak: measured only across a 400 ms window around the impact itself, so the figure given to the dispatcher belongs to that collision rather than to the largest bump seen earlier in the session.
03

The phone dashboard

The demo vehicle is moving, so every result belongs on a phone, not on a screen bolted to the car.

The board streams its status (current G, session peak, state, and countdown seconds) off-board five times per second. The call server renders it as a mobile web dashboard on the local network, so any phone can open it with no app install.

The instant an impact is confirmed the dashboard goes full-screen with the countdown and a large red CANCEL - I'M OK button, and the phone vibrates. One tap cancels and re-arms. The onboard pushbutton stays wired as a backup, and after an alert the dashboard offers a RE-ARM control.

  • Live telemetry: impact G and session peak, updated 5×/second
  • Ten-second cancel window: full-screen countdown with haptic feedback
  • Backup input: onboard hardware button mirrors the CANCEL action
  • Re-arm: return the system to monitoring after a cancelled or completed alert
04

Systems behind the call

Four subsystems turn a detected impact into a conversation a dispatcher can actually use.

Link

Wireless link

BLE GATTESP32Wi-Fi fallback

The ESP32 runs a BLE GATT server with three characteristics: crash alerts out, live status out, and phone commands (CANCEL / REARM) in. A Python bridge relays alerts upward and button presses back down. For noisy conference radio environments, a compile-time flag switches the board onto a phone hotspot and talks to the server over HTTP instead; each status POST returns any pending command, so no bridge is needed at all.

Context

Map intelligence

OpenStreetMapNominatimOverpass

A dispatcher asks things no profile can hold: what's the nearest cross street? what city is this? where's the closest ER? At the moment of the crash CrashGuard resolves the live GPS fix into a context bundle using key-less OpenStreetMap services.

  • One combined query: named roads, hospitals, and landmarks are fetched in a single Overpass request rather than three, cutting lookup latency and rate-limit exposure to roughly a third. That is what made cross streets reliable.
  • Mirror failover: several public Overpass endpoints are tried in turn, because any single one frequently rate-limits.
  • What it returns: street address, city, county and ZIP, nearest named roads, closest hospitals, and nearby landmarks (schools, fuel, pharmacies, police and fire stations, shops, tourist sites), each with distance and compass bearing computed by the haversine formula.
  • Explicit gaps: fields that come back empty are marked unavailable in the agent's context, so it states plainly that it does not have them instead of hedging.
  • Off the critical path: the lookup runs on a background thread while the phone rings, so it never delays the call, and the live coordinates are applied instantly at trigger time.
  • Continuous position: the phone captures live GPS automatically and continuously, because a crash victim cannot press a button. Browser geolocation requires HTTPS, and the last fix is cached on disk so it survives a server restart.
Voice

The AI dispatcher agent

Twilio VoiceClaude APIFlask

The Flask call server receives the crash event and uses Twilio to place the outbound call. It opens with a spoken briefing (name, GPS coordinates and nearest address, peak impact force, blood type, medical conditions, primary emergency contact), then listens. The dispatcher's speech is transcribed and handed to a Claude agent whose system prompt contains only the occupant profile and live crash data, instructed to answer in one to three short sentences, read numbers digit by digit, and say "I don't have that information" rather than ever guess.

Record

Incident documentation

SMSSMTPIntent parsing

CrashGuard produces a formatted report covering timestamp, peak impact, coordinates, address, cross streets, nearest hospitals, occupant identity, blood type, conditions, allergies, medications, emergency contacts, and vehicle details.

  • Published before it is sent: the report always goes to the phone dashboard first, before any send is attempted. That path cannot be blocked by a carrier, so the report is never lost regardless of what happens to SMS or email.
  • Delivery is verified, not assumed: Twilio accepting a message only means it was queued. US local (10DLC) numbers must be registered for A2P messaging or carriers silently drop the traffic, which looks like success in the API but never arrives. The system polls the message until it reaches a terminal status and reports the truth, naming the registration requirement when that is the cause.
  • Asked for at any point: a request for the report is recognised anywhere in the call, not only inside a scripted offer.
  • Spoken input parsed locally: phone numbers ("five seven five...") and email addresses ("chief at example dot gov") are decoded on the host. All intent handling is local rather than model-driven, so it adds no per-call inference cost and responds instantly.
Reliability

Keeping a live call from falling over

Most of the failure modes in this system are timing and lifecycle problems rather than algorithmic ones, so they are handled explicitly:

  • Inference off the webhook path: model inference is dispatched to a worker thread and the webhook returns immediately, so the telephony provider's roughly 15 second webhook timeout cannot terminate a live call during a slow inference.
  • Non-blocking trigger: the crash trigger returns instantly, with dialing and map enrichment running in parallel background threads, so the BLE bridge never times out waiting on the server.
  • BLE recovery: re-advertising is deferred to the main loop after a disconnect, since calling it inside the disconnect callback fails silently on the ESP32, and a heartbeat watchdog drops stale links so a bridge restart does not require power-cycling the board.
  • Startup self-check: every host module and dependency is verified present and from the same release, so version drift surfaces before a demo rather than mid-call.
  • Cost and latency control: a small fast model, prompt caching on the invariant system prompt, truncated conversation history, and short spoken replies.
05

Specifications & stack

Stack

What it is built from

  • MYOSA Mini Kit: ESP32 motherboard, MPU6050 (accelerometer only), buzzer and pushbutton on the I2C chain
  • Arduino (C++): firmware, official MYOSA sensor libraries, ESP32 BLE stack
  • Python 3 + HTML/JS: Flask call server, live mobile dashboard, bleak BLE bridge, pyserial calibration tooling
  • OpenStreetMap: Nominatim and Overpass for reverse geocoding, cross streets, and nearby hospitals (free, no API key)
  • Twilio Programmable Voice: outbound calling, speech recognition, neural text-to-speech
  • Claude API: grounded conversational dispatcher agent

06

Status & what's next

Roadmap

The full chain (detection, cancel window, BLE alert, AI call, map lookups, and incident reporting) runs end to end on the prototype above. Work continues on hardening the demo and extending the system:

  • Rollover detection from the gravity vector already computed at calibration, by detecting when the measured gravity direction inverts. No new sensor data is required.
  • Phone app to replace the laptop bridge, which would bring real phone GPS into the alert
  • LTE alert path for genuinely standalone operation with no host nearby
  • Additional language support for the dispatcher agent
